children.text: A planned new town built on the site of a former US and Philippine military base, with wide sidewalks, parks, large murals, and restaurants from around the world. It's a clean, safe city destination where you can enjoy everything on foot, from a stroll along High Street to The Mind Museum and the American Cemetery.

Bonifacio Global City (BGC) is a planned new town in Taguig City, southeast Metro Manila. The land was once "Fort William McKinley," a US military base under American rule, and after independence became "Fort Bonifacio," the headquarters of the Philippine military. Urban development began in the

when the Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) sold part of the base to private developers, and later Ayala Corporation and others built it into what it is today. The city takes its name from Andres Bonifacio, a leader of the Philippine Revolution.

BGC is rare among Metro Manila districts in being a "walkable city." Its grid streets, wide sidewalks, green spaces and parks scattered throughout, and drivers who actually stop at crosswalk signals make it easy to push a stroller or walk hand in hand with a child. Large murals and sculptures throughout the streets turn the whole city into an open-air gallery, and bright lighting at night draws many people out for an evening walk.

BGC is a business hub packed with offices of Philippine finance and IT companies and multinationals, and it's also a residential area for many Korean expatriates and their families. As a result, it has excellent restaurants and cafes from around the world, along with Korean restaurants and Korean grocery stores — making it a good place for an "easy day" during a longer trip.

There are no grand historic sites here, but it's recommended for travelers who want to see the Philippines' modern face and the life of its urban middle class, for those who enjoy shopping and dining out, and for families looking for somewhere safe to walk around with kids.
Chronologically, the land began as Fort William McKinley, established by the United States in
, and was renamed Fort Bonifacio when it became the headquarters of the Philippine Army in
. In
, the Fort Bonifacio Development Corporation (FBDC), a joint venture between the BCDA and the Metro Pacific consortium, took on the development of about 150 hectares, and in
Ayala Land took over the lead role in its development. Today BGC covers about 240 hectares, and its landmarks are Bonifacio High Street, opened in
, and the Metrobank Center, the tallest building in the Philippines (
tall, completed in
, and home to Grand Hyatt Manila). Taguig long disputed jurisdiction over the area with Makati City, but a Supreme Court ruling in
December 2021
upheld Taguig City's jurisdiction.

BGC's central street, with a long green park down the middle flanked by shops and restaurants on either side. Walking among the fountains and sculptures naturally leads to both a meal and some shopping.
Opened in

as the Philippines' first full-fledged science museum, it has more than 250 interactive exhibits across five galleries: Universe, Earth, Life, Atom, and Technology. "Stan," a large Tyrannosaurus skeleton replica, is a hit with kids. It's usually open Tuesday–Sunday,
9 AM–6 PM
, and closed on Mondays; allow
2–3 hours
to see everything.

blocks.title: Hunt for murals and public art

children.text: BGC's official public art guide lists 19 murals and sculptures. Icon Plaza (at the corner of 26th Street and 7th Avenue) has the mural "Between the Lines" by CYRCLE, an artist collective from Los Angeles, and sculptures by Reg Yuson stand at several entrances to High Street, so it's fun to track them down with a map app and take photos.

blocks.title: The Manila American Cemetery and Memorial

children.text: A World War II cemetery for fallen US soldiers south of BGC, with about 17,000 white crosses spreading endlessly across a grassy hillside. A quiet, solemn place to reflect on the history of the Pacific War.

Connected to Forbestown Road, Burgos Circle is a small circular park ringed by bars and cafes, with a lovely evening atmosphere. The park is home to "The Trees," BGC's first public sculpture, installed in
. Near High Street, the Serendra and Market! Market! area has a cluster of casual restaurants and souvenir shops.
A mall in McKinley Hill, south of BGC, where you can ride a gondola along a canal modeled on Venice, Italy. It's a nice spot to drop by for photos. Opened by Megaworld in
, the mall features a
canal and a replica of the Rialto Bridge; gondola rides cost extra, and weekend waits can be long.

From rooftop bars atop high-rise hotels and buildings, you can look out over the skylines of BGC and Makati. Visit around sunset to catch the moment the city lights come on. Top picks include Straight Up on the 22nd floor of Seda BGC and The Peak on the 60th–62nd floors of Grand Hyatt Manila; most require smart casual attire, and The Peak won't let you in wearing flip-flops.

Track 30th, at the corner of 30th Street and 7th Avenue, is a park with a jogging track and outdoor fitness equipment, plus the mural "Larong Pinoy," which depicts traditional Filipino games. Terra 28th is a garden-style park with shaded walking paths. Most BGC parks are open free of charge from
6 AM–10 PM
, making them great for a morning walk or a break with kids.

The BGC Bus is run by the Ayala-affiliated Fort Bonifacio Development Corporation (FBDC), with eight routes centered on the EDSA Ayala Terminal (McKinley Exchange Corporate Center, next to MRT Ayala station) and the Market! Market! Terminal. Most fares are

on the Arca South Express), and cash isn't accepted, so you pay with a beep card or GCash. If you don't have a card, you can buy a single-use QR ticket at the ticket booths in the two terminals, but not at stops along the way. Most routes run from
5–6 AM
until
10 PM
, and a Night Route operates at night. Routes and schedules change often, so check the information at the terminal before boarding.

Jeepneys don't enter BGC's inner streets and only run on outer roads such as C-5 and McKinley Road. Coming from Ayala Avenue, get off at the Washington–Ayala jeepney terminal (at the intersection of EDSA and McKinley Road) and walk to the BGC Bus terminal. The MRT is extremely crowded during the evening rush, so if you have luggage, Grab is recommended.

The easiest way is to get off at Ayala station on MRT Line 3 and take the BGC Bus East Express (bound for Market! Market!) or the North Route from the EDSA Ayala Terminal right next to it. You can pay for the bus with a beep card or GCash, and it takes about
15–30 minutes
to reach the area around High Street.
Most of BGC can be explored on foot. It's about a
10-minute
walk from High Street to The Mind Museum, and about
10 minutes
to Burgos Circle. The American Cemetery and Venice Mall are a bit farther, so Grab (about
) is convenient.

Major roads have dedicated bike lanes, and you can rent Moovr shared e-bikes and e-scooters through the app at docking stations around the area. Walking from the eastern edge to the western edge takes only about
15–20 minutes
, so during the day walking is often faster.
If you land at Clark International Airport, take a Genesis Transport P2P bus to a terminal in Manila (TriNoma or Cubao
, Ninoy Aquino International Airport Terminal 3
, PITX
), then switch to Grab. The bus takes about
2–3 hours
, and fares are cash only.
From provincial cities such as Cebu and Davao City, take a domestic flight to Ninoy Aquino International Airport in Manila (about
1 hour 20 minutes–1 hour 30 minutes
from Cebu), then follow the "From the airport" directions above to reach BGC.
With its many indoor malls and restaurants, BGC can be visited any time of year. The best time for walking is
December–February
, when evening temperatures around 25°C make outdoor strolls and terrace dining pleasant.
March–May
can push midday temperatures close to 35°C, so it's a good idea to split your day — malls and museums during the day, street walks after sunset.
During the
June–October

rainy season, afternoon showers are frequent, but good drainage means flooding inside BGC is rare. Still, the C-5 road and the EDSA area leading into BGC can see severe congestion during heavy rain, so allow extra travel time.
In
December
, large Christmas lights and decorations go up along High Street and throughout the streets, making it the most dazzling time of the year. In
, starting with the tree lighting on
November 15
, fireworks were held on 5th Avenue every Saturday at
through
November–December
, and on the night of
December 31

, 5th Avenue hosts "NYE at the 5th," a free New Year's countdown show, along with fireworks. Schedules change every year, so check BGC's official social media. At year-end, the malls and streets get very crowded and traffic becomes heavy. Also, every Saturday and Sunday from
, 5th Avenue (between 28th and 30th Streets) becomes a car-free street.

BGC is packed with business and upscale hotels. Five-star hotels like Shangri-La The Fort and Grand Hyatt Manila cost about
a night, while four-star hotels like Seda BGC run about
. Long-term visitors will also find plenty of Airbnb-style serviced apartments (about
a night). Lodging costs more here than in nearby districts, but the safety, cleanliness, and walkability make it especially popular with families.

The dining choices here are very broad. High Street and Uptown Mall are packed with Filipino fusion cuisine, Japanese food, Spanish tapas, American brunch, and bakery cafes. To try authentic Filipino food, look for a dedicated Filipino restaurant serving sisig, crispy pata (fried pork knuckle), and kare-kare. With so many Korean expatriates, Korean restaurants, Korean-style fried chicken shops, and Korean grocery stores are easy to find too. Outdoor food markets sometimes pop up on weekend evenings, though operating days and locations change often, so check local announcements.
A long-standing favorite is Wildflour Cafe + Bakery, which started in BGC in

and grew into one of Manila's signature brunch cafes. For a cheap meal, head to the Fiesta Market food court on the outer side of Market! Market! to sample Filipino street food. Market! Market! is a mall aimed at middle-class shoppers, so you can buy souvenirs and everyday goods relatively cheaply, and during the Christmas season a market of street stalls also sets up around the mall.
Cards are accepted almost everywhere in BGC, but carry around
in cash for jeepneys and small stalls.
Buying a beep card lets you ride both the BGC bus and Manila's light rail lines, which is convenient.
High Street and the malls have free Wi-Fi, but it's slow, so a local SIM or eSIM is a better choice.
Friday evenings bring the heaviest waits for restaurants and traffic, as people head out after work. Book popular restaurants in advance.
The Mind Museum is closed on Mondays, and buying tickets online in advance speeds up entry. Check the official website for prices and pass options.
The American Cemetery is a solemn place, so avoid revealing clothing, loud noise, and drone photography, and bring your passport since ID may be requested at the entrance.
Mural photos come out best in the soft light of morning or late afternoon.
Traveling outside rush hour (
7–9 AM
5–8 PM
) can save you a lot on Grab fares and time.
The Manila American Cemetery is open free of charge every day from
9 AM to 5 PM
and closes only on
December 25
and
January 1
. To also see the memorial's 25 mosaic maps of the Pacific War, allow more than
1 hour
Most BGC parks (High Street park, Track 30th, Terra 28th, and others) are open free of charge from
6 AM–10 PM
; dogs must be leashed, and owners must clean up after them.
At BGC intersections, turning vehicles often don't yield to pedestrians. Follow the walk signals and use the crosswalks, but look both ways once more before crossing.
BGC itself is one of the safest districts in Metro Manila, but watch for pickpockets in crowded malls and event venues.
On Fridays and around year-end, Grab requests pile up and waits can exceed
30 minutes
. Build in extra time to get home, or take the BGC bus.
Restaurant bills often add a service charge (usually 10%) and VAT (12%), so don't budget based on menu prices alone.
Watch out for heatstroke on midday outdoor walks, and also beware of feeling unwell from the sharp temperature swing between air-conditioned interiors and the outdoor heat.
Large no-smoking zones are designated on the streets, and smoking outside a designated spot can result in a fine.
In areas with lots of bars and clubs, don't accept drinks from strangers, and don't leave your drink unattended.
